causalMechanism.primaryVector: Systemic glucocorticoid therapy causes a characteristic posterior subcapsular cataract (PSC) through direct, receptor-mediated effects on the lens epithelium. Aqueous glucocorticoid reaches the lens and binds glucocorticoid receptors in epithelial cells at the anterior equator; the resulting changes in epithelial proliferation, migration, and differentiation disturb the orderly formation of lens fibers beneath the posterior capsule, where aberrant cells and disorganized crystallins accumulate. Biochemical correlates include altered crystallin expression and aggregation, disturbed ion and water transport with hydration of lens fibers, oxidative stress, and impaired antioxidant defenses; the opacities begin at the posterior pole, are typically bilateral, and may progress with continued exposure. Risk is related to dose, duration, and individual susceptibility (potency and route matter), and concurrent hyperglycemia may amplify lens damage. Quantitatively, in a 10-year population-based cohort of 3,654 adults with photographic lens grading, current users of oral corticosteroids had a substantially increased risk of incident posterior subcapsular cataract (odds ratio 4.11, 95% CI 1.67-10.08) and nuclear cataract (OR 3.45, 95% CI 1.26-9.43), with no increased cortical cataract risk; users of both inhaled and oral corticosteroids had an adjusted odds ratio of 4.76 (95% CI 2.59-8.74) for PSC cataract. A systematic literature review of 32 studies of long-term systemic corticosteroid exposure lists cataract (1-3% prevalence) among the common toxicities, alongside fracture (21-30%), hypertension (more than 30%), and gastrointestinal and metabolic adverse events, and notes that dose-duration risk relationships remain poorly quantified. The classic literature review documents the well-established association between corticosteroid therapy and posterior subcapsular cataract while cautioning that published series do not establish a simple dose-threshold relationship because of individual lens susceptibility. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so a visually significant PSC cataract developing on documented chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where a pre-existing cataract is documented, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the systemic corticosteroid regimen (drug, prednisone-equivalent daily dose, cumulative duration, dates), the lens findings with slit-lamp or photographic documentation and posterior subcapsular morphology, the chronology of steroid exposure relative to opacity development, and the measured visual effect; exclude or account for age-related nuclear or cortical cataract (the subtype not associated with steroids in the cohort above), diabetes, smoking, ultraviolet exposure, ocular trauma, uveitis or intraocular inflammation, and prior ocular surgery.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Systemic glucocorticoids produce bone loss through direct effects on bone cells and bone vascularity, and the risk appears early in treatment. Glucocorticoids reduce the lifespan and function of osteoblasts and osteocytes, shift bone remodeling toward resorption, suppress gonadal and growth-hormone axes, and reduce bone vascularity, so that bone strength falls more than bone mineral density alone would predict; trabecular-rich sites such as the vertebrae and femoral neck are affected disproportionately, and bone loss is fastest in the first months of therapy. The fracture risk is dose-dependent and detectable even at low doses and with short courses, which matters for veterans treated with repeated steroid bursts for a service-connected inflammatory condition. Quantitatively, a cohort of 244,235 oral corticosteroid users matched to 244,235 controls found dose-dependent fracture risk: relative rate of hip fracture 0.99 (95% CI 0.82-1.20) at prednisolone doses under 2.5 mg/day, rising to 1.77 (1.55-2.02) at 2.5-7.5 mg/day and 2.27 (1.94-2.66) at 7.5 mg/day or more; vertebral fracture rates rose in parallel from 1.55 to 2.59 to 5.18; and a nationwide cohort of 1,548,945 adults found that 21.1% received short-term oral corticosteroids and that fracture risk was increased within 30 days of initiation (incidence rate ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.69-2.07), persisting at prednisone-equivalent doses below 20 mg/day. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so glucocorticoid-induced osteopenia (reduced bone mineral density and/or fragility fracture) developing on documented systemic corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where reduced bone density predates the steroid exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the steroid regimen (drug, prednisone-equivalent dose, duration, cumulative exposure, dates), dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry results with T-scores and dates, fracture history with imaging, and the chronology of exposure relative to bone loss; and address competing causes — postmenopausal and age-related bone loss, hypogonadism, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D and calcium deficiency, malabsorption, chronic kidney disease, smoking, alcohol, other medications (proton-pump inhibitors, anticonvulsants, aromatase inhibitors), and immobilization. The rating proceeds by analogy under § 4.20 to DC 5013 because no code specifically addresses osteopenia.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Corticosteroids raise intraocular pressure and produce secondary open-angle glaucoma by increasing resistance to aqueous humor outflow through the conventional pathway — the trabecular meshwork, the juxtacanalicular connective tissue, and the inner wall of the Schlemm canal. Glucocorticoids induce extracellular matrix deposition (including myocilin and fibronectin) and cytoskeletal changes in trabecular meshwork cells that reduce outflow facility, so intraocular pressure rises; in susceptible individuals the steroid response progresses from asymptomatic ocular hypertension to sustained pressure elevation, glaucomatous optic neuropathy, and irreversible visual-field loss if the elevation is unrecognized or continues. The effect is a class property of corticosteroids rather than of any one drug or route: it has been recognized since the 1950s after systemic ACTH and both topical and systemic corticosteroids, risk increases with prolonged use, higher frequency, higher anti-inflammatory potency, and greater ocular penetrance (and is greater in children and in known steroid responders), and reducing the molecule's intrinsic steroid activity (as with loteprednol etabonate) demonstrably reduces the intraocular pressure effect. Under 38 CFR § 3.310(a), a disability proximately due to or resulting from the treatment of a service-connected condition is itself service-connected, so corticosteroid-induced ocular hypertension and glaucomatous damage developing on documented corticosteroid therapy for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis is a treatment-complication secondary claim; where pre-existing open-angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension is documented before steroid exposure, § 3.310(b) limits service connection to the attributable aggravation. For an 'at least as likely as not' opinion, document the corticosteroid regimen (drug, route, potency, frequency, duration, dates — including topical ocular and periocular injections, which carry the highest ocular risk), serial intraocular pressure measurements and optic-nerve and visual-field examinations with dates, the chronology of pressure rise relative to steroid exposure, and the response to steroid withdrawal or pressure-lowering therapy; and address competing causes — primary open-angle glaucoma (family history, age, myopia, African ancestry, diabetes), angle-closure mechanisms, uveitis and other intraocular inflammation, pseudoexfoliation, and pigment dispersion. Because the diagnosis is open-angle glaucoma unless the mechanism is angle closure, the claim is evaluated under DC 6013 (or DC 6012 for angle closure) — the requirement for a diagnostic code is met directly rather than by analogy.

causalMechanism.primaryVector: Pharmacological sequence: chronic systemic glucocorticoid therapy prescribed for service-connected rheumatoid arthritis suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis through negative feedback, reducing corticotropin (ACTH) secretion and adrenal cortisol output; secondary (tertiary) adrenal insufficiency may become clinically apparent during tapering or after withdrawal and may persist long after the drug stops. Younes and Younes (PMID 29184808) describe this mechanism directly and note that HPA-axis recovery after cessation is variable and can take 6-12 months. Broersen et al. (PMID 25844620) pooled 74 articles and 3,753 adult corticosteroid users tested for adrenal insufficiency: pooled percentages varied by route from 4.2 percent (nasal) to 52.2 percent (intra-articular) and by disease from 6.8 percent (inhaled-only asthma) to 60.0 percent (hematologic malignancy), with a dose gradient; oral therapy falls within this range. Bowley et al. (PMID 41521083) systematically reviewed only studies using protocolised systemic glucocorticoid regimens and ACTH-stimulation testing, reporting that adrenal insufficiency is a common complication of systemic glucocorticoid therapy with considerable variability; the retrieved abstract excerpt did not expose a pooled estimate, so none is claimed here. These sources establish treatment-mediated causation at the mechanism level while showing that individual risk depends on route, dose, duration, potency, tapering and host factors; no single percentage can be applied to a veteran.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: obtain the exact corticosteroid agent(s), route, dose, cumulative duration, taper schedule and stop dates; concurrent topical, inhaled or intra-articular exposure; morning cortisol or ACTH-stimulation results; symptoms such as fatigue, orthostasis, nausea, hyponatremia; and any adrenal-crisis or continued-steroid-dependence events. Document whether insufficiency predated steroid therapy — primary adrenal disease, pituitary pathology, prior pituitary surgery or radiation, opioid effects, checkpoint-inhibitor effects — as competing causes; a pre-existing or independently caused insufficiency changes the theory from § 3.310(a) causation to § 3.310(b) aggravation of a baseline. Recovery testing after withdrawal informs severity and permanence but is not a prerequisite to attributing the insufficiency to treatment.

Legal and rating analysis: 'Medication Side Effect' is treatment-mediated secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a): service-connected rheumatoid arthritis leads through documented corticosteroid exposure to HPA suppression and adrenal insufficiency. If pre-existing adrenal insufficiency was worsened by necessary steroid therapy, analyze aggravation under § 3.310(b) with a documented baseline and attributable decrement beyond the natural course. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion needs the individual's exposure and endocrine chronology plus competing-cause exclusion placing the evidence at least in approximate balance; pooled prevalence does not itself meet that standard. Original proposal mechanism (preserved verbatim):
Inflammatory-structural sequence: in service-connected rheumatoid arthritis, chronic synovitis erodes the midfoot and hindfoot joints (talonavicular, subtalar and naviculocuneiform) and attacks the tibialis posterior tendon sheath, weakening the dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch; the combination of joint destruction and posterior tibial tendon dysfunction allows progressive valgus collapse of the hindfoot and midfoot — acquired flatfoot. Bouysset et al. (PMID 12022347) obtained weight-bearing radiographs of 308 feet in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and 202 control feet, and found that flat foot increased markedly after three to four years of disease duration, with forefoot deformity progression tracked alongside. Zhao et al. (PMID 39421746), applying bidirectional Mendelian randomization and mediation analysis in European populations, found genetic evidence consistent with rheumatoid arthritis causally contributing to postural deformities including flat foot, and their review of the literature reported flat-foot prevalence of roughly 11.0 to 42.1 percent in rheumatoid arthritis. Mizuki et al. (PMID 41053714) analyzed rheumatoid foot deformity patterns and reported flat foot and hindfoot valgus deformities in the range of 19 to 43 percent, emphasizing that coronal hindfoot alignment drives forefoot deformity. These sources establish rheumatoid arthritis as a recognized cause of acquired flatfoot at population and genetic-instrumental levels; observational and genetic designs cannot determine whether any individual veteran's arch collapse is attributable to the arthritis rather than to an independent cause.

Required individual evidence and competing causes: document the rheumatoid arthritis by diagnosis and disease duration with inflammatory activity, and characterize the flatfoot with weight-bearing radiographs or clinical measurement of arch height, hindfoot valgus, tenderness and tibialis posterior function; note whether the deformity is flexible or fixed because that determines both mechanism and rating. Congenital or hereditary pes planus, posterior tibial tendon dysfunction unrelated to inflammatory disease, tarsal coalition, Charcot arthropathy (including diabetic Charcot), obesity and mechanical overload, prior trauma or fracture, and tibialis posterior rupture from other causes are competing causes that must be assessed. A temporal sequence in which a previously normal arch collapses after years of active seropositive rheumatoid disease, with radiographic joint erosion and tibialis posterior dysfunction, favors the rheumatoid route; a lifelong flatfoot or a deformity that develops without active inflammatory disease and without joint erosion points to another cause.

Legal and rating analysis: this is direct secondary causation under 38 CFR § 3.310(a) when the service-connected rheumatoid arthritis produces the acquired flatfoot; the theory is causation because a new structural foot disability is generated by the inflammatory disease. If a pre-existing flatfoot or arch insufficiency is asserted to have been worsened, a separate § 3.310(b) aggravation analysis must identify the qualifying baseline (earlier imaging or examination) and the attributable increment beyond natural progression. An 'at least as likely as not' opinion requires the disease duration and activity, the radiographic erosion pattern, the tibialis posterior findings and the competing-cause analysis to be weighed so that the evidence is at least in approximate balance; prevalence figures and Mendelian randomization do not establish an individual probability. No individual probability is asserted here. Rating: § 4.71a DC 5276 is the dedicated acquired-flatfoot code, while the primary is rated under DC 5002 during active disease and DC 5003 for chronic residuals; the Note to DCs 5013-5024 is not the operative route for acquired flatfoot. Apply § 4.14 so that the same arch collapse, foot pain or weight-bearing limitation is not rated under both DC 5276 and a DC 5003 residual limitation for the same foot, and apply § 4.25 and the bilateral factor where both feet are separately impaired. Landing this incoming route requires host-file review: the rheumatoid-arthritis host identity is published and currently points to depressive disorder and GERD, and the flatfoot identity is draft with an outbound association-only suggestion to osteoarthritis and no inbound edges for this inflammatory route.
